claims.text: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 can be prepared in a homogenized high-temperature BCC state.
Phase stability in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 is governed jointly by the thermodynamic driving force for phase separation and the kinetics of atomic mobility.
The thermodynamic driving force for phase separation reflects composition-dependent Gibbs free-energy differences.
Diffusion limitation during rapid cooling prevents phase separation and preserves metastable BCC Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7.
Slow cooling or isothermal annealing below the homogenization temperature provides more time for atomic rearrangement.
Increased atomic mobility permits local compositional fluctuations to overcome kinetic barriers and initiate nucleation and growth.
The phases nucleated during slow cooling or annealing will include lower-energy FCC phases or intermetallic compounds.
Rapidly quenched Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 should remain predominantly BCC with minimal detectable secondary phases.
Slow-cooled or annealed Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 should contain more FCC or intermetallic secondary phase than the rapidly quenched baseline.
Greater thermal exposure should produce morphological changes such as grain growth or phase segregation that correlate with atomic mobility.
The controlled comparison keeps composition and starting microstructure fixed while varying only cooling rate or annealing protocol.
The rapidly quenched sample serves as the baseline intended to retain the high-temperature BCC phase.
The proposed mechanism is restricted to a temperature regime in which BCC is initially present and diffusion-controlled processes dominate.
The critical cooling rate and identities and sequences of the secondary phases are not specified.
Failure of slow-cooled or annealed samples to show a statistically significant increase in secondary phases relative to the quenched baseline would falsify the proposed mechanism.
